syllabus_version: Issue 3 (as on the cover; footer: Specification – Issue 3 – September 2024). First teaching September 2017, first examination June 2019. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE in Biology (4BI1).
page_reference_note: All page references in this map are PDF page numbers. The printed page number on content pages is the PDF page minus 6 (e.g. PDF p. 17 = printed p. 11).
tier_notes: Untiered (PDF p. 7). Every student sits both papers in the same series (PDF p. 7). Paper 1 (4BI1/1B) assesses the content that is not in bold and does not have a 'B' reference; Paper 2 (4BI1/2B) assesses all the content, including content that is in bold and has a 'B' reference; bold statements cover some sub-topics in greater depth; on both papers questions may come from any topic area across the specification (PDF pp. 13-14, 33). In this map tier 'core' = statement with no B suffix (Paper 1 and Paper 2 content); tier 'supplement' = statement with a B suffix (Paper 2 only). The website labels these 'Paper 1 & 2' and 'Paper 2 only'. The specification states that bold 'B' statements are content only in the International GCSE in Biology and not in the International GCSE in Science (Double Award) (PDF p. 7). Paper 1 code is shared with Science (Double Award) as 4SD0/1B (PDF pp. 13, 43).
paper_notes: Both papers: externally assessed written examinations set and marked by Pearson, availability November and June, first assessment June 2019; a mixture of different question styles, including multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, calculations and extended open-response questions; a calculator may be used (PDF pp. 13-14, 33). Total 180 marks (110 + 70), marks not scaled; grades 9 to 1 (PDF p. 33). AO weightings for the qualification: AO1 Knowledge and understanding of biology 38-42%; AO2 Application of knowledge and understanding, analysis and evaluation of biology 38-42%; AO3 Experimental skills, analysis and evaluation of data and methods in biology 19-21%. Paper 1: AO1 23.2-25.7%, AO2 23.2-25.7%, AO3 11.6-12.8%; Paper 2: AO1 14.8-16.3%, AO2 14.8-16.3%, AO3 7.4-8.2% (PDF p. 35). Experimental skills are assessed through the written examinations (PDF pp. 7, 34).

command_words.Add/Label: Requires the addition or labelling of a stimulus material given in the question, for example labelling a diagram or adding units to a table.
command_words.Calculate: Obtain a numerical answer, showing relevant working.
command_words.Comment on: Requires the synthesis of a number of variables from data/information to form a judgement.
command_words.Complete: Requires the completion of a table/diagram.
command_words.Deduce: Draw/reach conclusion(s) from the information provided.
command_words.Describe: To give an account of something. Statements in the response need to be developed, as they are often linked but do not need to include a justification or reason.
command_words.Determine: The answer must have an element that is quantitative from the stimulus provided, or must show how the answer can be reached quantitatively. To gain maximum marks, there must be a quantitative element to the answer.
command_words.Design: Plan or invent a procedure from existing principles/ideas.
command_words.Discuss: Identify the issue/situation/problem/argument that is being assessed within the question; Explore all aspects of an issue/situation/problem/argument; Investigate the issue/situation etc. by reasoning or argument.
command_words.Draw: Produce a diagram either using a ruler or freehand.
command_words.Estimate: Find an approximate value, number or quantity from a diagram/given data or through a calculation.
command_words.Evaluate: Review information (e.g. data, methods) then bring it together to form a conclusion, drawing on evidence including strengths, weaknesses, alternative actions, relevant data or information. Come to a supported judgement of a subject’s quality and relate it to its context.
command_words.Explain: An explanation requires a justification/exemplification of a point. The answer must contain some element of reasoning/justification – this can include mathematical explanations.
command_words.Give/State/Name: All of these command words are really synonyms. They generally all require recall of one or more pieces of information.
command_words.Give a reason/reasons: When a statement has been made and the requirement is only to give the reason(s) why.
command_words.Identify: Usually requires some key information to be selected from a given stimulus/resource.
command_words.Justify: Give evidence to support (either the statement given in the question or an earlier answer).
command_words.Plot: Produce a graph by marking points accurately on a grid from data that is provided and then draw a line of best fit through these points. A suitable scale and appropriately labelled axes must be included if these are not provided in the question.
command_words.Show that: Verify the statement given in the question.
command_words.Sketch: Produce a freehand drawing. For a graph, this would need a line and labelled axes with important features indicated. The axes are not scaled.
command_words.State what is meant by: When the meaning of a term is expected but there are different ways for how these can be described.
command_words.Suggest: Use your knowledge to propose a solution to a problem in a novel context.
command_words.Analyse the data/graph to explain: Verb preceding a command word: Examine the data/graph in detail to provide an explanation.
command_words.What, Why, Which: Direct command words used for multiple-choice questions.

given: None stated: the specification does not list any data sheet, formula sheet, equation list or periodic table for either paper (checked PDF pp. 7-8, 13-14, 33-35, 43-55).

Students will be expected to have access to a suitable electronic calculator for all examination papers; calculators that allow the retrieval of text or formulae, or with QWERTY keyboards, are not allowed (PDF p. 34; also pp. 13-14).

Any numerical data, organism-specific information or unfamiliar context needed for a question must therefore be supplied in the question itself (inference from the absence of any data sheet; not stated in the specification).
not_given: Word equation and balanced chemical symbol equation for photosynthesis: 'know' (2.18-2.19). The specification does not print the equations; standard forms: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy, chlorophyll); 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

Word equation and balanced chemical symbol equation for aerobic respiration in living organisms: 'know' (2.37). Not printed; standard forms: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

Word equation for anaerobic respiration in plants and in animals: 'know' (2.38). Not printed; standard forms: animals glucose → lactic acid; plants (and yeast, 5.5-5.6) glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. No balanced symbol equation is required for anaerobic respiration.
Human diploid chromosome number 46 and haploid number 23 (3.32).
Sex chromosomes XX in a female and XY in a male (3.26).
DNA base pairing: adenine (A) with thymine (T), cytosine (C) with guanine (G); RNA contains uracil (U) instead of thymine (3.16B, 3.17B, Paper 2 only).
About 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (4.9).
Magnesium ions needed for chlorophyll, nitrate ions for amino acids (2.22).

Meanings of the terms in 3.20 (dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, phenotype, genotype), 3.21B (codominance), 3.14 (genome, gene), 4.1 (population, community, habitat, ecosystem), 4.3B (biodiversity), 2.56B (transpiration), 2.81 (homeostasis), 3.34 (mutation), 5.16 (transgenic).
Greenhouse gases named in 4.13: water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, methane and CFCs.

Mathematical skills in Appendix 4 ticked for Biology are 'developed and assessed' and not given (PDF pp. 49-50), including calculating areas of triangles and rectangles, surface areas and volumes of cubes (5C).

No magnification equation and no other quantitative biology formula appears in the 4BI1 content; any formula needed for a calculation is not on the specification's recall list, so it should be supplied in the question (inference).
conventions: Paper 2-only statements are printed in bold with a 'B' suffix on the statement number (PDF pp. 7, 13-14, 33).
Practical investigations are specification points in italics, beginning 'practical:' (PDF pp. 7, 34).
The word 'including' in the content helps specify the detail of what must be covered (PDF p. 7).
Examples in the content are for illustrative purposes only; centres can use other examples (PDF p. 7).

Generic and species names are printed in italics in the content: Mucor, Amoeba, Chlorella, Plasmodium (1.2), Lactobacillus bulgaricus, Pneumococcus (1.3), Lactobacillus (5.7); 'in vitro' is italicised (5.17B). The specification states no rule on binomial naming.
Specific names of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle are not required (4.11B).

British spelling and the specification's terms, e.g. haemoglobin, oesophagus, oestrogen, fertilisation, specialised, organisation, co-ordination, micro-organisms, sulfur dioxide, hydrogen-carbonate indicator, geotropic, phototropic, vasoconstriction, vasodilation, glomerular filtrate, Bowman’s capsule, loop of Henle, proximal convoluted tubule, nitrogen fixing bacteria, pyramids of number, pyramids of energy transfer.
Assessment is in English only (PDF p. 37).
The specification states no rules on units, significant figures or number formatting beyond Appendix 4 skill 2A 'Use an appropriate number of significant figures' (PDF p. 49).
appendices: Appendix 1 Codes (PDF p. 43): subject code 4BI1; paper codes 4BI1/1B (also 4SD0/1B) and 4BI1/2B.

Appendix 4 Mathematical skills (PDF pp. 49-50), skills ticked for Biology (B column): 1A decimal form; 1B standard form; 1C ratios, fractions, percentages, powers and roots; 1D estimates without a calculator; 2A appropriate number of significant figures; 2B arithmetic mean; 2C bar charts; 2D frequency tables, diagrams and histograms; 2E principles of sampling; 2F simple probability; 2G mode and median; 2H scatter diagram pattern or trend; 2I order of magnitude calculations; 3B change the subject of an equation; 3C substitute numerical values into algebraic equations using appropriate units; 3D solve simple algebraic equations; 4A translate between graphical and numerical form; 4C plot two variables from experimental or other data; 4D slope and intercept of a linear graph; 5C areas of triangles and rectangles, surface areas and volumes of cubes. NOT ticked for Biology: 1E sin x; 3A symbols <, >, ∝, ~; 4B y = mx + c; 4E tangent slope as rate of change; 4F area under a curve; 5A angular measures; 5B 2D/3D representation.
Appendix 5 Command word taxonomy (PDF pp. 51-52): see command_words; 'What, Why, Which' are the direct command words for multiple-choice questions.

Appendix 6 Suggested practical investigations (PDF p. 53): additional, non-numbered suggestions (e.g. reaction times, effect of exercise on heart rate, enzymes in washing powders, glucose in simulated urine, sampling with pooters, sweep nets, pitfall traps); not specification statements and not mapped.
Appendix 7 Glossary (PDF p. 55): administrative terms only (assessment objectives, external assessment, JCQ, linear).

Experimental skills that may be tested in the written papers (PDF p. 34): solve problems in a practical context; apply knowledge in practical contexts; devise and plan investigations; demonstrate or describe methods including safe practical techniques; observations and measurements with appropriate precision, recorded methodically and presented appropriately; identify independent, dependent and control variables; analyse and interpret data to draw conclusions consistent with the evidence; communicate findings with technical language, calculations and graphs; assess reliability; evaluate data and methods taking into account accuracy and validity.

topics.topic_name: The nature and variety of living organisms

points.text: understand how living organisms share the following characteristics:; they require nutrition; they respire; they excrete their waste; they respond to their surroundings; they move; they control their internal conditions; they reproduce; they grow and develop.

describe the common features shown by eukaryotic organisms: plants, animals, fungi and protoctists; Plants: these are multicellular organisms; their cells contain chloroplasts and are able to carry out photosynthesis; their cells have cellulose cell walls; they store carbohydrates as starch or sucrose. Examples include flowering plants, such as a cereal (for example, maize), and a herbaceous legume (for example, peas or beans). Animals: these are multicellular organisms; their cells do not contain chloroplasts and are not able to carry out photosynthesis; they have no cell walls; they usually have nervous co-ordination and are able to move from one place to another; they often store carbohydrate as glycogen. Examples include mammals (for example, humans) and insects (for example, housefly and mosquito). Fungi: these are organisms that are not able to carry out photosynthesis; their body is usually organised into a mycelium made from thread-like structures called hyphae, which contain many nuclei; some examples are single-celled; their cells have walls made of chitin; they feed by extracellular secretion of digestive enzymes onto food material and absorption of the organic products; this is known as saprotrophic nutrition; they may store carbohydrate as glycogen. Examples include Mucor, which has the typical fungal hyphal structure, and yeast, which is single-celled. Protoctists: these are microscopic single-celled organisms. Some, like Amoeba, that live in pond water, have features like an animal cell, while others, like Chlorella, have chloroplasts and are more like plants. A pathogenic example is Plasmodium, responsible for causing malaria.
points.diagram_note: organism features are often shown as drawings or photographs; can be given as text descriptions

points.text: describe the common features shown by prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria; Bacteria: these are microscopic single-celled organisms; they have a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm and plasmids; they lack a nucleus but contain a circular chromosome of DNA; some bacteria can carry out photosynthesis but most feed off other living or dead organisms. Examples include Lactobacillus bulgaricus, a rod-shaped bacterium used in the production of yoghurt from milk, and Pneumococcus, a spherical bacterium that acts as the pathogen causing pneumonia.
points.diagram_note: bacterial cell structure often shown as a drawing; can be described in words

points.text: understand the term pathogen and know that pathogens may include fungi, bacteria, protoctists or viruses; Viruses: these are not living organisms. They are small particles, smaller than bacteria; they are parasitic and can reproduce only inside living cells; they infect every type of living organism. They have a wide variety of shapes and sizes; they have no cellular structure but have a protein coat and contain one type of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA. Examples include the tobacco mosaic virus that causes discolouring of the leaves of tobacco plants by preventing the formation of chloroplasts, the influenza virus that causes ‘flu’ and the HIV virus that causes AIDS.

understand the biological consequences of eutrophication caused by leached minerals from fertiliser
understand the effects of deforestation, including leaching, soil erosion, disturbance of evapotranspiration and the carbon cycle, and the balance of atmospheric gases
describe how glasshouses and polythene tunnels can be used to increase the yield of certain crops
understand the effects on crop yield of increased carbon dioxide and increased temperature in glasshouses
understand how the use of fertiliser can increase crop yield
understand the reasons for pest control and the advantages and disadvantages of using pesticides and biological control with crop plants
understand the role of yeast in the production of food including bread
practical: investigate the role of anaerobic respiration by yeast in different conditions

points.text: understand the role of bacteria (Lactobacillus) in the production of yoghurt

understand the use of an industrial fermenter and explain the need to provide suitable conditions in the fermenter, including aseptic precautions, nutrients, optimum temperature and pH, oxygenation and agitation, for the growth of micro-organisms

understand how selective breeding can develop plants with desired characteristics
understand how selective breeding can develop animals with desired characteristics
